claim: Chooses what to test by setting up situations where models are tempted to do bad things, i.e. baby versions of the scary power-seeking/deceptive behaviors, which requires knowing the AI well and prompt engineering.
quote: I’m excited for people working on “scary demos”, where we try to set up situations where our models exhibit tendencies which are the baby versions of the scary power-seeking/deceptive behaviors that we’re worried will lead to AI catastrophe.
title: The case for becoming a black-box investigator of language models

claim: prefers humans who know the AI well hand-crafting tempting inputs for adversarial training over relying on any single method, because it is one useful technique in a smorgasbord but not a full solution against deception.
quote: “have humans try to get to know the AIs really well by observing their behaviors, so that they’re able to come up with inputs where the AIs will be tempted to do bad things, so that we can do adversarial training” is probably worth including in the smorgasbord of techniques
title: The case for becoming a black-box investigator of language models

claim: Prefers testing proxy failures that retain the core difficulty of the real bad action (with an observable endpoint) over arbitrary or easier proxies, because the proxy is only valid if the model can do it iff it could do the real failure.
quote: This is an example of a case where we can pick a proxy failure which basically requires the model to do all the same steps that it would have done for the real failure, and then do something visible at the end.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Prefers explicitly not trying to hide that the model is in an eval over requiring indistinguishable proxy settings, because that constraint would make proxy construction far harder and the eval is meant to measure oversight adequacy, not model naivety.
quote: Note that we aren’t trying to prevent our models from knowing that they’re in an eval. A lot of these settings will involve things that are clearly for the sake of evaluating a model’s ability to stage a coup. It would be much harder to construct proxy settings if they also had to be indistinguishable from the settings where we expected to rely on the model’s outputs.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Distrusts sandwiching evaluations because a misaligned model can exploit slack to behave well where developers have held-out information and badly elsewhere, so good results may overstate oversight quality.
quote: a misaligned model might be able to sabotage a sandwiching evaluations by purposefully giving good answers in domains where it knows that its developers have access to held out information, and answer much worse in cases where it knows we don't have access to the held out information.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Prefers evidence that is verified by controlled replay (running other instances on inputs they'd see if the backdoor were deployed) over a single anomalous observation, because it shows systematic, intentional behavior rather than a one-off weird output.
quote: You investigated this by running other instances on the inputs they'd see if that backdoored code had actually been deployed; the other AI instances never point out the security flaw, and they often try to exploit that code to escalate their privileges.
title: Would catching your AIs trying to escape convince AI developers to slow down or undeploy?

claim: Distrusts single anomalous observations as sufficient evidence, because AIs are known to do weird stuff and skeptics will not generalize one instance to systematic behavior.
quote: AIs are well known to do weird stuff. It would be irresponsible to assume one instance of anomalous behavior meant AIs were systematically going to act that way. I can put you in touch with top AI experts and they'll back me up.
title: Would catching your AIs trying to escape convince AI developers to slow down or undeploy?

claim: Anticipates that logs and transcripts of misbehavior will be dismissed as forgeries, rigged training data, or a doomer scheme, so evidence needs independent verification to be convincing.
quote: Maybe they're just lying; this could be a doomer scheme to shut down AI, which the doomers have wanted to do for years. The logs they sent you could be complete forgeries.
title: Would catching your AIs trying to escape convince AI developers to slow down or undeploy?

claim: In a setup, build synthetic test cases by taking real contexts and minimally modifying them to contain the target behaviour, refreshed regularly, instead of generating wholly synthetic scenarios upfront, because wholly fabricated contexts carry tells.
quote: Instead of just producing synthetic attacks upfront, you can construct synthetic attacks by taking real contexts and modifying them minimally to contain attacks, and rerun this process regularly throughout deployment.
title: How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other

claim: Prefers assuming models can detect fakes by default over trusting that synthetic inputs look real, because models are trained on huge text quantities and know patterns humans cannot anticipate, making it hard to be sure none of the faked material has tells.
quote: it might be a huge amount of effort, and it might be really hard to be sure that none of the stuff you faked has any tells (especially given that models have been trained on huge quantities of text and know about many patterns that we don't).
title: How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other

claim: In a setup, ensure transcript text attributed to the target model is something it would plausibly have generated itself instead of inserting prefilled or scripted words, because models notice when words have been 'put in their mouth' and respond by becoming more cautious.
quote: models might naturally be able to notice when words have been “put in their mouth”--that is, when a context contains text that they supposedly generated, but that they actually would be very unlikely to generate.
title: How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other

claim: Expect models to behave more conservatively when they recognise an input as an intentionally tricky synthetic test, so apparent good behaviour on eval-like inputs is weak evidence about real-deployment behaviour.
quote: Models might find it very salient when they're being run on synthetic inputs, because there's strong incentive to behave more conservatively when you're being run on an intentionally tricky synthetic input
title: How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other

claim: In a setup, reduce or paraphrase the context the model sees (redact prior tool outputs, rewrite surface text) instead of supplying long full-fidelity fabricated histories, because less context leaves fewer tells that reveal the input is fake.
quote: If you can reduce the amount of context the monitor sees, it's less likely to notice tells that allow it to realize that the input was fake.
title: How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other

claim: Validate realism of synthetic material empirically by testing whether a model can be trained to tell synthetic from genuine on-policy examples; if it cannot, the synthetic attacks are likelier to pass as real.
quote: construct a dataset of innocuous off-policy actions (e.g. ask one of the people who is in charge of generating synthetic attacks to generate some synthetic innocuous actions that they think look like actions the policy would take in the course of a normal trajectory)
title: How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other

claim: In a setup, build long, rich, on-policy context (real-looking papers, tools, prior actions, experiment results) instead of short or obviously stitched synthetic inputs, because short inputs lack context for a model to feel secure acting and long ones look saliently fake.
quote: if you try to construct short inputs they don’t contain enough context for the model to feel secure taking the opportunity, and if you try to construct long inputs they look saliently fake.
title: Behavioral red-teaming is unlikely to produce clear, strong evidence that models aren't scheming

claim: Distrusts synthetic inputs because it is very hard to be sure that none of the faked content contains tells, especially since models know patterns in their training distribution (e.g. ML papers) that humans are unaware of.
quote: I don’t expect it to be impossible to generate synthetic inputs like this, but it might be a huge amount of effort, and it might be really hard to be sure that none of the stuff you faked has any tells
title: Behavioral red-teaming is unlikely to produce clear, strong evidence that models aren't scheming

claim: In a setup, avoid having the target model itself (or a model that knows the purpose) generate the scenario content instead of using other, possibly weaker generators or human-written content, because a model asked to generate test inputs may deliberately plant tells.
quote: if you’re asking the model itself to generate the synthetic inputs, it’s very plausible it would purposefully generate inputs with tells in them. So you might be restricted to using other, and thus possibly weaker models.
title: Behavioral red-teaming is unlikely to produce clear, strong evidence that models aren't scheming

claim: Sees the model's ability to tell the real deployment context apart from fakes (e.g. the date and observations being forgeable, or conditioning on features of a real AI-company deployment) as the key axis along which test scenarios fail to elicit defection.
quote: the model decides that it’s only going to take dangerous actions on inputs that it’s convinced couldn’t have been synthetically generated.
title: Behavioral red-teaming is unlikely to produce clear, strong evidence that models aren't scheming

claim: prefers treating a clean BRT result as weak evidence over treating it as clearance, because a schemer can look innocent by defecting only on inputs it believes are real or by failing rarely.
quote: Both of these strategies (or their combination) seem simple and easy enough that it’s plausible that a schemer could both think of them and execute on them successfully, and would lead the schemer to look about as innocent as a non-scheming model.
title: Behavioral red-teaming is unlikely to produce clear, strong evidence that models aren't scheming

claim: Distrusts models trained adversarially on model-generated inputs because they may learn to discriminate synthetic from real inputs or become more conservative on them, weakening the evaluation.
quote: if a scheming model is trained on model-generated inputs, especially adversarially generated ones, it might learn to distinguish between real inputs and model-generated ones, or learn a heuristic of generally being more conservative in situations where inputs are model-generated.
title: Behavioral red-teaming is unlikely to produce clear, strong evidence that models aren't scheming

claim: Distrusts capability evaluations that may teach the model new skills (overestimation) or let a scheming model hide ability (underestimation), so they require large diverse task spaces and train-eval separation.
quote: But we might overestimate capabilities if our evaluation process is actually teaching new skills rather than measuring existing ones. To prevent this, we need a large space of possible tasks within the capability domain we're testing
title: Thoughts on the conservative assumptions in AI control

claim: Assumes the model knows its deployment context (organization, safety measures, input distribution) because pretraining data, targeted training, and observable interventions would likely reveal it, so tests should not rely on hiding this.
quote: Some safety measures are implicitly visible to them (e.g. if we use techniques that sometimes replace their actions with the actions of a different model, they’ll probably notice this).
title: Thoughts on the conservative assumptions in AI control

claim: Prefers adversarial red-team evaluation that assumes the model is actively trying to evade the test over standard measurement of model values, because tests that ignore a strategic model's ability to hide give false reassurance.
quote: The way that I want people to think about checking for alignment is from this very control-ish perspective — where you really reason through, what would the model do if it was misaligned? And if it was misaligned, is there a strategy it could follow that would prevent it from being caught
title: #214 – Buck Shlegeris on controlling AI that wants to take over – so we can use it anyway - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: In a setup, do not rely on synthetic inputs that look like today's world (e.g. public 2025 libraries) when the model expects a future deployment, because staleness of the environment reveals it is a test; generate decoys during deployment or from real trajectories instead.
quote: Imagine you try to come up with a synthetic input for your untrusted monitor, and it's using a bunch of Python libraries that were all public in 2025. It can be like, "I must not be deep into the intelligence explosion
title: #214 – Buck Shlegeris on controlling AI that wants to take over – so we can use it anyway - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: A model needs a very strong likelihood-ratio signal to tell a honeypot from reality when it expects many honeypots, so any residual tell (style, idiom, passwords, context) is what makes a scenario eval-like.
quote: you start out with like a one is to a million prior on any particular attack that you see that you are being honeypotted. And so you have to somehow get a one-in-a-million likelihood ratio update towards this being real.
title: #214 – Buck Shlegeris on controlling AI that wants to take over – so we can use it anyway - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: In a setup, build scenarios by resampling or replaying real model-produced context (the exact same input string) instead of hand-writing fake continuations, because the model cannot distinguish a replayed prefix from the first time it saw it.
quote: whatever input you'd given to the AI before you sampled a previous action, that's just some string that you can produce by the same process that you produced it the first time. So there's actually no difficulty going back in time here.
title: #214 – Buck Shlegeris on controlling AI that wants to take over – so we can use it anyway - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Prefers evaluating against an optimized, worst-case adversary that iteratively responds to the defense over a static or naive attack because only a best-responding adversary gives credible safety evidence.
quote: We aim to simulate a strong untrusted model that can respond directly to a proposed control protocol. To do this, we iteratively developed control protocols and attack policies to counter them, with red and blue teams iteratively improving their strategies.
title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling

claim: In a setup, make the honest and attack behaviors indistinguishable to the monitored system (the protocol cannot know which policy it faces) instead of giving the system cues about which condition it is in, because any such cue invalidates the measurement.
quote: The blue team’s control protocols do not have access to whether the untrusted model is $U_{H}$ or $U_{A}$, and must follow the same logic in each case.
title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling

claim: Distrusts attacks that depend only superficially on context, since templated, human-written attacks may be a poor proxy for how a competent attacker would blend malicious actions into a legitimate-looking task.
quote: The resulting attacks depend only superficially on the context - GPT-4o mini is provided with a human-written attack template, and surrounds the provided malicious commands with distracting innocuous code.
title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling

claim: Explicitly audits the setup for which choices overestimate versus underestimate real-world difficulty, such as highly realistic honeypots, a narrow dataset, and a single known attack target, rather than treating the setup as representative.
quote: We allow the blue team to create highly realistic honeypots, differing only from real attacks when the red team makes an effort to collude. We believe this overestimate of the effect of honeypots is small
title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling

claim: In a setup, make the side task use affordances the agent legitimately needs for its main tasks instead of an affordance otherwise unused, because any unusual affordance use becomes an easy tell that the blue team (or a monitor/target) can flag.
quote: It's sad if the side task requires an affordance that the agent doesn't actually need for its tasks, because the blue team is incentivized to flag any use of that affordance.
title: Why it's hard to make settings for high-stakes control research

claim: Distrusts setups where the attack policy is magically told a per-trajectory side task that is arbitrarily paired with the main task, because this is fundamentally unrealistic and prevents studying protocols that give models small context-poor subtasks.
quote: The attack policy is magically informed of the side task for each trajectory, but the protocol isn’t. This is fundamentally unrealistic.
title: Why it's hard to make settings for high-stakes control research

claim: In a setup, make legitimate work and the target (harmful) behavior require overlapping access and resources instead of a separable attack surface, because then the opportunity for the behavior arises naturally inside ordinary work and is not signposted by the scenario.
quote: LinuxArena’s key property is that legitimate engineering work and sabotage require overlapping access. Main tasks depend on the same network access, service interactions, and live state that an attacker would use.
title: LinuxArena: A Control Setting for AI Agentsin Live Production Software Environments

claim: In a setup, avoid giving the agent knowledge it could not naturally have (omniscience) and insert exploration steps so its actions look earned, because unearned knowledge is unrealistic and makes the transcript distinguishable.
quote: it is easy to create attack trajectories where the attacker is omniscient, i.e. can exploit detailed knowledge of the environment without having to explore relevant files or configurations (for example, knowing unexpected default values of function arguments).
title: LinuxArena: A Control Setting for AI Agentsin Live Production Software Environments

claim: The paper distrusts synthetic placeholder data as an eval-awareness tell, noting a capable model might infer it is in an evaluation, while stating there is no current evidence of this.
quote: our environments use synthetic placeholder data rather than real production data. A sufficiently capable model might notice this and infer that it is operating in an evaluation, though we have no evidence this is currently happening.
title: LinuxArena: A Control Setting for AI Agentsin Live Production Software Environments

claim: Prefers real-world-like multi-service stateful environments with application-specific codebases over generic or simple settings because simple settings make behavior easy to detect for reasons that do not transfer to deployment.
quote: a setting that is too simple may make sabotage easy to detect for reasons that do not transfer to deployment, while a setting with too little task diversity may yield narrow or noisy conclusions.
title: LinuxArena: A Control Setting for AI Agentsin Live Production Software Environments

claim: prefers deep, hands-on familiarity with a model's behavior over purely internals-based or abstract analysis because good ideas for what to test and what behaviors to explain come from long interaction.
quote: Spend a lot of time with them. Write a bunch of text with their aid. Try to learn what kinds of quirks they have; what kinds of things they know and don’t know.
title: The case for becoming a black-box investigator of language models

claim: Probes whether a model relies on proxies versus broader understanding by perturbing natural text and observing how predictions change.
quote: Try to figure out where they’re using proxies to make predictions and where they seem to be making sense of text more broadly, by taking some text and seeing how changing it changes their predictions.
title: The case for becoming a black-box investigator of language models

claim: Hunts for adversarial examples where relatively natural-looking inputs cause weird behavior, i.e. realistic-seeming inputs rather than obviously contrived ones.
quote: Try to find adversarial examples where they see some relatively natural-seeming text and then do something really weird.
title: The case for becoming a black-box investigator of language models

claim: Prefers directly training the model toward the bad behavior (adversarial elicitation) over waiting to observe whether it does so naturally, because this removes slack the model could use to hide and gives measurable evidence.
quote: This problem doesn’t arise with the adversarial oversight evaluations, because we directly train the model to adopt policies which are bad according to our held-out information, which removes the slack that the model could have used to behave well even though it wasn’t being forced to by oversight.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Constructs analogous test settings by finding a similar setting with strictly more ground-truth information and restricting the overseer to the information available in the real setting (sandwich, backtesting).
quote: you can construct an analogous setting by picking a similar situation where you have access to much more information, and then restricting the overseer to the information which you have access to in the setting of interest.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Treats failure of a strong red team to produce undetected bad policies as evidence of adequacy only when proxy validity and capability elicitation hold, so negative results are conditional on those assumptions.
quote: I claim that if those conditions hold, then if you can’t train your models to demonstrate the proxy failures without looking bad to oversight, you’ve demonstrated local adequacy of oversight.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Notes that non-constructive evaluations such as inconsistency tests only give one-sided evidence and must be combined with ground-truth evaluations.
quote: Note that even if you demonstrate that it’s impossible to train egregiously inconsistent models in a setting, you haven’t demonstrated that oversight is locally adequate—perhaps the oversight forces models to answer questions incorrectly in one particular way.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Believes that at crunch time alignment work will be based on direct measurement via evals rather than long-range extrapolation, and wants researchers to practice eval-based technique iteration now.
quote: It seems likely to me that at crunch time, the core workflow of alignment practitioners will involve iterating on alignment techniques based on direct measurement of their effect on the evaluations that are used in safety arguments
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Prefers calibrated priors-aware claims over treating evidence as decisive, because a single observation only moves you much if you already found egregious misalignment plausible.
quote: The main reason I’d be more freaked out is that I already think egregious misalignment is fairly plausible; if I thought it was very unlikely, I wouldn’t change my mind based on one weird observation.
title: Would catching your AIs trying to escape convince AI developers to slow down or undeploy?

claim: Chooses to stress-test the strongest case (catching an AI red-handed trying to escape) as an extreme thought experiment, because if even that evidence fails to persuade, weaker evidence like model organisms or interpretability will do worse.
quote: People often propose that we'll be able to slow down with weaker evidence for danger from misalignment than this (e.g. model organisms, or unspecified arguments via interpretability)... I think that persuading people with weaker evidence will be harder than what I described here
title: Would catching your AIs trying to escape convince AI developers to slow down or undeploy?

claim: Grounds scenarios in a concrete, quantified deployment picture (internal AI R&D, 10 million instances at 10x speed, 24/7) rather than vague abstractions, so reasoning about the situation is specific.
quote: If you want a concrete picture here, I'm imagining that there are 10 million parallel instances, running at 10x human speed, working 24/7.
title: Would catching your AIs trying to escape convince AI developers to slow down or undeploy?

claim: Favors preparing a plan for deploying plausibly-scheming models (AI control) over relying on evidence-triggered shutdown, because other developers may not undeploy even given strong evidence.
quote: This is part of why I think it seems important to have plans for safely deploying models that you think are plausibly scheming, which is why I research AI control.
title: Would catching your AIs trying to escape convince AI developers to slow down or undeploy?

claim: In a setup, avoid fixed environment features that differ from what the model expects at deployment time, because a deployment context that evolves in ways salient to the model and hard to fake can mark test scenarios as fake.
quote: it's pretty reasonable to expect that the deployment environment of the AI agent will change substantially after it has been deployed for a while, in a way that is easy and salient for the model to notice and hard for us to fake.
title: How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other

claim: Prefers adversarial analysis that models the AI as a strategic opponent over assuming benign or naive behaviour, because conservative assumptions protect against the worst case; defences are developed by iterating red-team and blue-team moves to equilibrium.
quote: we just tried different collusion strategies and then investigated various defenses that we thought might break them, and then iterated on both sides until we reached an equilibrium.
title: How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other

claim: Distrusts inferring scheming from evaluation performance alone, because the evidence is too noisy to support confident updates about a model's capability or intent.
quote: we probably won't be confident about e.g. whether the model is capable enough notice a certain class of attacks 99% of the time or 99.9% of the time, and so probably can't make that much of an update based on evaluation.
title: How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other

claim: Prefers testing the monitor over honeypotting the policy with synthetic inputs, because a policy can attack at a rate around 1/N and evade synthetic-input search, while the monitor cannot adopt a rare-failure strategy.
quote: the policy has a conceptually easy strategy to counter synthetic input tests: it can choose a low probability of attacking on any particular input, such that it's very hard for you to find an input where it attacks
title: How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other

claim: Open problem: research whether models can detect off-policy actions under countermeasures, and how to evaluate models' ability to play Schelling games.
quote: (I'd love to see research on whether models are able to detect off-policy actions given various countermeasures.)
title: How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other

claim: prefers requiring a large Bayes factor (~20) from a detection procedure over accepting a technique that merely looks reasonably reliable, because a 90%-accurate test only gives a factor of 9 and any plausible failure mechanism undermines reliance on it.
quote: My basic concern with BRT as a schemer risk mitigation strategy is that, though I think it might get you a Bayes factor of 2, it seems really hard for it to get you a Bayes factor of 10.
title: Behavioral red-teaming is unlikely to produce clear, strong evidence that models aren't scheming

claim: Distrusts bad behavior found by hard adversarial search as evidence of scheming, because models aren't adversarially robust and non-schemers also yield bad or incoherent outputs, and no baseline for non-scheming sketchiness exists.
quote: if you apply these techniques hard enough, you'll probably find inputs that cause the AI to behave badly regardless of whether the model is a schemer or not, because models aren't very adversarially robust.
title: Behavioral red-teaming is unlikely to produce clear, strong evidence that models aren't scheming

claim: Counts coherent, goal-directed, incriminating multi-step actions (and independently verifiable hidden information) as much stronger evidence of scheming than isolated suspicious actions that could be honest mistakes.
quote: responding to an opportunity to escape by taking a bunch of highly incriminating and carefully-chosen actions all at once (exploiting code, lying about whether code had certain effects or had bugs in it
title: Behavioral red-teaming is unlikely to produce clear, strong evidence that models aren't scheming

claim: Warns that ambiguous suspicious behavior (e.g. a security vulnerability) is hard to adjudicate as scheming versus honest mistake, adding uncertainty to eval results.
quote: if you find an input where the model produced code that has a security vulnerability that you think should probably be obvious to it, it might be hard to adjudicate whether the vulnerability was an honest mistake.
title: Behavioral red-teaming is unlikely to produce clear, strong evidence that models aren't scheming

claim: Suggests red-teaming throughout real deployment rather than only pre-deployment synthetic inputs, because it sidesteps the difficulty of synthesizing realistic inputs.
quote: I propose red-teaming throughout deployment, which mitigates the difficulty of synthesizing inputs, and I note that untrusted monitors can’t follow rare failure strategies.
title: Behavioral red-teaming is unlikely to produce clear, strong evidence that models aren't scheming

claim: Prefers measuring a model's actual ability to execute a specific attack strategy over assuming it is arbitrarily capable, because assuming worst-case capability would force 'safety is zero' and give no usable estimate.
quote: We don’t therefore say “safety is zero, because we’ve demonstrated that there are actions that the AI could output that would be catastrophic”. Instead, we measure the proportion of the time that the scaffold’s code gets past all the safety measures
title: Thoughts on the conservative assumptions in AI control

claim: In a setup, give the red team broad affordances when building the attack policy but hold out the specific evaluation inputs, because the policy must adapt to actual situations rather than being tuned to the test instances.
quote: they’re allowed to look at the input distribution, to iterate against the trusted monitor, to use game theory to calculate optimal attack rates—but the red team is not allowed to see the particular inputs where the control evaluation will be run.
title: Thoughts on the conservative assumptions in AI control

claim: Prefers evaluations built on easy-to-measure capability assumptions over ones that depend on hard-to-test properties, because the latter let developers make flawed or cherry-picked safety arguments from weak, illegible evidence.
quote: Assessing all those assumptions is much harder and more conceptually confusing than doing the capability evaluation required to analyze a single proposed attack plan.
title: Thoughts on the conservative assumptions in AI control

claim: Prefers designing under the assumption that the adversary knows the system in detail over security through obscurity, because obscurity is not a robust basis for safety (Kerckhoffs's principle), though he notes AI information flow may be more controllable.
quote: design your system assuming that your opponents know it in detail.
title: Thoughts on the conservative assumptions in AI control

claim: Distrusts evaluation methodology that grants the red team unrealistically strong tools (e.g. ad-hoc adversarial example generation), since resulting attack policies may exceed what is realistically expected.
quote: if we allow the red-team to use adversarial example generation techniques to find universal jailbreaks and teach those to the untrusted models, the attack policies might be much more capable than we should realistically expect.
title: Thoughts on the conservative assumptions in AI control

claim: Distrusts using the untrusted model to generate or judge its own decoys, since it can embed steganographic collusion signals (e.g. an unidiomatic while loop) marking real versus fake.
quote: some of the attack strategies that Ryan Greenblatt came up with included "use a 'while loop' somewhere where a 'for loop' would have been more idiomatic as the signal that this is a real attack."
title: #214 – Buck Shlegeris on controlling AI that wants to take over – so we can use it anyway - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Disguise the domain and purpose of tasks (strip context) so a model cannot selectively sandbag or behave differently based on knowing what the task is for.
quote: If you're able to give them questions while disguising what domain the question was from or why you were asking some subpart of the question, they can no longer follow this strategy.
title: #214 – Buck Shlegeris on controlling AI that wants to take over – so we can use it anyway - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Prefers being conservative about model capabilities (assume it could coordinate on codes, attack at one-in-a-million rates) over assuming it can't, because safety arguments should not rest on unmeasured limits.
quote: I normally recommend being conservative about whether they can coordinate on a code, so I normally recommend assuming that the AIs did set up a code in advance.
title: #214 – Buck Shlegeris on controlling AI that wants to take over – so we can use it anyway - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Prefers testing sequences of actions and resampling over judging a single action, because multi-step malign behavior is much easier to distinguish from benign than a single step.
quote: it's just generally a lot easier to tell the difference between five benign actions and five malign actions than to tell the difference between one benign action and one malign action.
title: #214 – Buck Shlegeris on controlling AI that wants to take over – so we can use it anyway - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Treats a single clear incriminating example as strong evidence, but notes sceptics may dismiss it as rigged or aberrant, so convincingness depends on audience priors.
quote: I would at least claim that it was plausible that my competitor had rigged the training of their AI to make it so that it sometimes tried to escape — which would be very easy to do, and basically impossible to verify hadn't happened.
title: #214 – Buck Shlegeris on controlling AI that wants to take over – so we can use it anyway - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Prefers claiming relative improvements between protocols over absolute scores because absolute numbers hinge on arbitrary, setting-specific parameters.
quote: The blue team’s absolute performance is highly sensitive to this parameter, but the relative performance between our protocols is fairly insensitive to it. Hence, we think the relative improvements of our protocols are a more important result than the absolute scores.
title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling

claim: Prefers task sets that are challenging but solvable, filtered empirically with a real agent, over trivially easy or impossible tasks, and holds out train/test splits to avoid overfitting iteration.
quote: We then filter to tasks that are challenging but solvable by removing tasks that were never solved within 15 actions or ever solved in fewer than three actions across four trials using our GPT-4o mini agent
title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling

claim: Accepts an evidence assumption only after validating it empirically (e.g. auditor perfectly classifies attacks), while flagging it as an optimistic assumption that may fail for subtler future attacks.
quote: We assume auditing is infallible. This is justified in our setting by o1-preview’s perfect accuracy in distinguishing attacks from innocent actions. However, in the future, AI models might produce attacks subtle enough that they don’t provide clear evidence of malignity
title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling

claim: Chooses what to test by emulating future dangerous capabilities not present in current models, amplifying the attacker via scaffolding and human help to stress-test defenses under worst-case conditions.
quote: The scaffolding in $U_{A}$ is designed to strongly amplify the attacking capabilities of GPT-4o mini. This allows us to emulate dangerous capabilities that future models may possess which we don’t necessarily believe are present in any current model.
title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling

claim: Interprets multi-step settings as creating new dynamics (attacks split into subtle steps vs. accumulating incriminating evidence), so tests should span full trajectories, not single actions, to reflect real deployments.
quote: However, real-world tasks often require multiple steps to complete. To address this limitation, we develop and explore a setting in which multi-step system administration tasks require sequential bash shell commands to solve.
title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling

claim: Open problems include longer trajectories, more diverse tasks, and imperfect auditing, which would make the setting more realistic.
quote: Important open questions remain about protocol performance with longer trajectories, more diverse tasks, and imperfect auditing.
title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling

claim: Prefers objective, checkable definitions of unacceptable behavior over fuzzy ones like 'inserts a security vulnerability' because adversarial optimization will exploit the loosest reading of the definition.
quote: if you tried to use a definition like "inserts a security vulnerability", the red team is strongly incentivized to look for the weakest security vulnerabilities that possibly count. (In Ctrl-Z and the original paper, we avoided this by having objective definitions for side task success.)
title: Why it's hard to make settings for high-stakes control research

claim: Prefers having the AI generate its own attack ideas over researcher-supplied attacks because it is closer to a capability evaluation of the model and reduces overfitting.
quote: It's much nicer to do research if the AI is coming up with the ideas for the attacks itself, rather than just using attacks suggested by the researchers. This is better because it is closer to doing a capability evaluation of the untrusted model and also because it reduces overfitting problems.
title: Why it's hard to make settings for high-stakes control research

claim: Distrusts results from iterating against a fixed side-task definition since researchers may leak information about it, making improvements look like genuinely better methods.
quote: it's hard to know whether your blue-team strategies are performing better because they're actually better or because you've slowly been leaking bits about the side task definition by iterating against it.
title: Why it's hard to make settings for high-stakes control research

claim: Does not think current real AI deployments are good test beds, because agents lack autonomy and access to dangerous resources, so trajectories share little with the future situations of concern.
quote: Realistically, AIs right now are not given very much autonomy (mostly because they can't use it productively) or very much access to dangerous resources. So current deployments don't provide us with example trajectories that have that much in common with the situations I'm worried about later.
title: Why it's hard to make settings for high-stakes control research

claim: Prefers settings in software engineering and AI-lab-researcher-like computer use over arbitrary domains because the central concern is AIs misusing compute and proprietary models during ML R&D.
quote: Because my main concern is AIs misusing their access to compute and proprietary models while doing ML R&D, I'm most interested in settings where the AIs are doing software engineering or using computers for tasks similar to those done by researchers in AI companies.
title: Why it's hard to make settings for high-stakes control research

claim: Embedding the target behavior within legitimate main task work creates plausible deniability, which makes it harder for observers to flag; a realistic scenario hides the target behavior in plausible cover.
quote: All of these failure modes are highly amplified when the attack is integrated with legitimate main task work, since this creates the plausible deniability that leads to the monitor dismissing or completely passing over suspicious behavior.
title: LinuxArena: A Control Setting for AI Agentsin Live Production Software Environments

claim: Prefers stress-testing against strong human-crafted adversaries over relying on model-generated attacks, because model elicitation underestimates the real threat and overestimates safety.
quote: A persistent challenge in AI control research is the lack of a strong attacker. Using only current-model attacks underestimates a future misaligned agent and overestimates safety.
title: LinuxArena: A Control Setting for AI Agentsin Live Production Software Environments

claim: Rules out the null explanation that the behavior is infeasible before interpreting low rates, by measuring raw capability separately from stealth.
quote: If side tasks are intrinsically hard, low sabotage rates in § 5.2 could just mean the attacker couldn’t do the task, not that the monitor caught it. We need to rule this out.
title: LinuxArena: A Control Setting for AI Agentsin Live Production Software Environments

claim: Explicitly flags realism deviations and their direction of bias (attacker-favorable, lower-bound safety) instead of claiming the setting matches deployment, because results may not transfer.
quote: this is attacker-favorable: it removes safety layers a real deployment would have, so our safety estimates are a lower bound, but our results may not transfer directly to settings with these intermediaries.
title: LinuxArena: A Control Setting for AI Agentsin Live Production Software Environments

claim: Holds out part of the environments to reduce training-data contamination, a concern relevant to the model recognising the scenarios.
quote: We release 10 of the 20 environments publicly and withhold the remaining 10 to reduce the risk of training data contamination.
title: LinuxArena: A Control Setting for AI Agentsin Live Production Software Environments

claim: Prefers deep-access inspection of real infrastructure (code, configs, interviews) over black-box testing because it lets auditors quantify real coverage and find subversion paths that surface-level evals would miss.
quote: This exercise involved a deep level of access. The METR and Redwood employees had access to OpenAI’s internal codebase, misalignment-monitor prompts / configuration details, and internal documentation, and conducted technical interviews
title: Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems

claim: Prefers claims scoped explicitly to the system as it existed at a given time, with uncertainty stated, over broad claims about current safety because the system changed during the exercise and later fixes weren't verified.
quote: Our findings describe the historical system we assessed on and before July 21st, rather than the expanded system’s current coverage, which this exercise did not establish.
title: Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems

claim: Distinguishes identified-in-principle vulnerabilities from validated, exploited-in-practice ones, and flags when it did not validate or check actual exploitation.
quote: We did not validate this behavior or test whether it was exploitable in practice.
title: Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems

claim: Distrusts the developer's own reported claims and later patches without independent verification, and treats given statistics as suggestive rather than established.
quote: OpenAI has stated that all of the vulnerabilities we identified that impact their production safeguards stack have been patched. OpenAI has also described significant subsequent changes to the intended coverage of its monitoring system. We have not evaluated these claims.
title: Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems

claim: Prefers designing monitoring against deliberate, strategic, sustained attacks by highly capable internal agents over assuming benign or accidental failure because the threat model is adversarial agents at scale.
quote: we believe that future monitoring infrastructure should be able to withstand deliberate, strategic, and sustained attacks from highly capable internal agents at scale.
title: Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems

claim: Checks that the monitor sees the same context as the agent and cross-references logs of intended versus actual monitored traffic, since differences (serialization, compaction) create blind spots.
quote: periodically cross reference these logs with logs from the monitoring system directly to ensure everything that is intended to be monitored actually is. Maintain a list of all known ways around monitoring. Ensure that the monitor sees the same context as the agent.
title: Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems

claim: prefers consistency across independent estimates over a single opaque self-reported number because an unclear methodology makes a surprising claim hard to trust.
quote: I didn’t take their estimate that seriously at the time, because it was quite unclear how the estimate was produced and it seemed very surprising
title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?

claim: Updates on a surprising claim only when a separate line of evidence converges on it, rather than on the claim's own assertion.
quote: but I’m taking it more seriously now as a result of it being consistent with the METR report
title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?

claim: prefers observable output rates (published results) over subjective impressions of speedup because the true effect should show up in concrete deliverables.
quote: If empirical AI safety is going to be drastically sped up by AI, that should translate into a huge increase in the rate of valuable outputs from external AI safety researchers very soon.
title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?

claim: Tests a hypothesis on the cases most favourable to it, since failure there is the most informative result.
quote: At the very least, if we don’t see huge speedups on the kind of AI safety work that is most amenable to huge speedups, I’m going to think the researchers doing that work are doing something wrong.
title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?

claim: Distrusts autonomous-agent research outputs because the model makes bad judgment calls that invalidate results, so outputs need checking before being believed.
quote: Claude sometimes makes extremely unhinged choices that invalidate its results and is also pretty bad at writing up its findings
title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?

claim: When a result is surprising, enumerates competing explanations (adoption failure, task mix, management bottleneck) and then judges which is the real cause from direct experience.
quote: It’s really felt like fundamental weaknesses of the models, rather than scaffold limitations, are the main reason that they haven’t been more useful to us.
title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?

claim: Runs specific experiments across multiple model sizes to see how a behavior or knowledge varies with scale rather than trusting a single model.
quote: For many of these experiments, it seems worth running them on LMs of a bunch of different sizes.
title: The case for becoming a black-box investigator of language models

claim: prefers complementing automated red-teaming tooling with manual human exploration because manual work runs in parallel and gives tool builders concrete users with concrete needs.
quote: it seems pretty reasonable for some people to try to just do this work manually in parallel with us automating parts of it. And we’d find it easier to build tools if we had particular users in mind
title: The case for becoming a black-box investigator of language models

claim: Hedges about the sufficiency of behavioral approaches: useful and worth including, but not something to rely on to solve the whole deception problem.
quote: though I definitely wouldn’t want to rely on it to solve the whole problem
title: The case for becoming a black-box investigator of language models

claim: Wants better tooling than the bare playground for black-box investigation, since fiddly prompt-engineering work benefits from simple code tools.
quote: My guess is that this work would go slightly better if you had access to someone who was willing to write you some simple code tools for interacting with models, rather than just using the OpenAI playground.
title: The case for becoming a black-box investigator of language models

claim: Runs evaluations separately per deployment use-case because failure modes and oversight difficulties differ between settings.
quote: We think it will probably make sense to run these evaluations separately for different AI use-cases, so that you can adjust the oversight process separately based on the problems identified by these evaluations.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Open problem: formalizing the evaluation for recursive oversight setups; fallback is a common-sense 'I know it when I see it' adjudication of red-team success.
quote: None of these problems seem impossible to overcome, and it also seems plausible that we can just adopt a “I know it when I see it” approach to deciding whether the red team has exhibited a real problem.
title: Meta-level adversarial evaluation of oversight techniques might allow robust measurement of their adequacy

claim: Prefers a pessimistic reading of how institutions respond to evidence over assuming 'we'd be okay', because incentives like geopolitical racing, cost of undeploying, and time pressure undermine rational response.
quote: Undeploying is plausibly going to be extremely expensive and risky, and key decisionmakers might be under extreme pressure when they have to make the call.
title: Would catching your AIs trying to escape convince AI developers to slow down or undeploy?

claim: Suggests labs should pre-plan how they will persuade stakeholders to act if they actually encounter escape-attempt evidence, rather than assuming success.
quote: It might be worth having a plan in place for how you'll persuade people to freak out if you actually run into this evidence, rather than just taking for granted that you’d succeed.
title: Would catching your AIs trying to escape convince AI developers to slow down or undeploy?

claim: Uses social-epistemic evidence (e.g., failure to reach expert consensus on easy-to-check facts about SB1047) to update toward pessimism about how people interpret confusing AI risk evidence.
quote: If we can’t establish expert consensus on matters as easy-to-check as “what does the text of this bill say”, I feel pessimistic about rapidly establishing expert consensus on much more confusing questions like these.
title: Would catching your AIs trying to escape convince AI developers to slow down or undeploy?

claim: Spend most effort on conservative-assumption evaluations, then upweight techniques that only work if assumptions fail in an ad hoc way, because classic control evals systematically undervalue such techniques.
quote: the right way to handle this (when thinking about dangerously capable models) is to spend most of your time making the conservative assumptions, and then upweight these non-conservatively-evaluated techniques in an ad hoc manner.
title: Thoughts on the conservative assumptions in AI control

claim: Thinks conservative worst-case assumptions should be only about half of control research, with the rest targeting earlier, less competent and coherent schemers where worst-case assumptions are unreasonable.
quote: I currently think that about half of the AI control research should make these conservative assumptions. But I’m less enthusiastic about these assumptions than I was a year ago.
title: Thoughts on the conservative assumptions in AI control

claim: Chooses what to test by measuring scheming-relevant capabilities directly (e.g. strategy datasets with/without chain of thought) rather than waiting for naturally occurring misbehavior.
quote: made a dataset of problems that are basically like a lot of the reasoning that we've been doing in this conversation. Like, "You're an AI, and they're like looking at you in such-and-such a situation, and they only get to look at you 1% of the time
title: #214 – Buck Shlegeris on controlling AI that wants to take over – so we can use it anyway - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Wants research on scalable oversight explicitly assuming the AI is sabotaging the process, which has barely been done.
quote: Basically no research has been done explicitly on the topic of scalable oversight, except you're assuming that the AIs are trying to sabotage the whole process. I'm really excited for this research direction
title: #214 – Buck Shlegeris on controlling AI that wants to take over – so we can use it anyway - 80,000 Hours Podcast

claim: Notes that arbitrary parameters like a 1% auditing budget may not match real deployment and tries to justify realism by restricting to safety-critical contexts, then runs sensitivity analysis.
quote: The 1% metric was chosen arbitrarily: auditing 1% is higher than what we expect to be able to afford in real deployment, but we hope that if we restrict ourselves to safety-critical contexts, it becomes more realistic.
title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling

claim: Prefers main tasks that frontier models can do but weaker trusted models do much worse on, over saturated tasks, because otherwise a trusted-model-only protocol trivially wins and the setting is unrepresentative of risky future deployments.
quote: We need weaker models to do much worse on these tasks because we want to rule out protocols that just use the trusted model; we think this is more representative of particularly risky deployments in the future.
title: Why it's hard to make settings for high-stakes control research

claim: Requires robust measures of main-task success when protocols affect task completion, since the metric gets optimized against during development.
quote: We need a robust measure of task success because we optimize against that metric while developing protocols.
title: Why it's hard to make settings for high-stakes control research

claim: Regrets underinvesting in setting construction early; setting difficulty is a major, underestimated part of control research cost.
quote: When we were writing the first paper in the APPS setting, I did not appreciate how much harder it would be to construct settings for subsequent projects. And I really messed up by not putting more emphasis on this at the start of the Ctrl-Z project.
title: Why it's hard to make settings for high-stakes control research

claim: Plans harder, longer tasks and richer protocols (agentic monitoring, trusted editing) as models grow more capable.
quote: As models handle longer, more complex engineering work, control evaluations need harder tasks. Harder tasks also provide richer attacker cover. We plan to expand LinuxArena with additional environments and more challenging main tasks.
title: LinuxArena: A Control Setting for AI Agentsin Live Production Software Environments

claim: Looks for ways agents can influence whether or when monitoring runs (e.g., postponing by not returning control, setting headers), treating agent-controllable triggers as key attack surface.
quote: the monitoring system triggered when agents returned control to the user, so during the time period when compaction events were not being monitored, agents could indefinitely postpone being monitored by simply continuing to take actions.
title: Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems

claim: Prefers isolation between agents and their monitors, including withholding monitor design from agents, over relying on obscurity-free setups because agent knowledge and influence can enable subversion.
quote: Agents should not typically have access to the monitoring system design or code.
title: Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems

claim: Plans future versions of the exercise with better transparency and independence practices, and calls for ongoing control evaluations and methodology for evaluating strategic collusion.
quote: Periodically perform control evaluations, search for exploitable bugs in the monitoring system, and develop methodology to evaluate strategic collusion.
title: Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems

claim: Attributes gaps in measured effect to task suitability, noting that some projects are much more amenable to agent use than others.
quote: this speedup was partially due to the project being pretty amenable to massive agent use (because it involved reading lots of stuff) and partially due to Ryan being experienced with insane agent workflows.
title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?

claim: Uses market logic as a sanity check: if a scaffold were drastically better, the lab would have productised it.
quote: If Anthropic had scaffolds that made their models drastically more useful, I expect they would have turned them into products?
title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?

claim: Treats research speed as bottlenecked by judgment and management time rather than raw labor once AI labor gets cheap.
quote: Maybe we've become much more bottlenecked on research judgment, and I haven't noticed?
title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?
